questions.title: How does FeatLLM extract rules from the LLM without fine‑tuning?
questions.question_body: In the paper, FeatLLM is described as using in‑context learning to make the LLM generate "rules" for each class. I am unclear on the exact prompting strategy that forces the model to produce these deterministic rule statements instead of directly outputting class predictions. Specifically, how does the two‑step reasoning instruction (Step 1: infer causal relationships, Step 2: deduce rules) avoid the model simply memorising spurious correlations from the few-shot examples? Could someone walk through a concrete example prompt and the expected LLM response format?

questions.title: What is the mathematical role of the non‑negative weight constraint in Eq. (2)?
questions.question_body: The authors define the class logit as `logit_k^i = max(w_k, 0) · z_k^i` and then apply a softmax. Why is `max(w_k, 0)` (i.e., projecting weights onto the non‑negative orthant) necessary? Does it have any theoretical justification beyond preventing "negative evidence" from a rule, and how does it affect gradient updates during the few‑shot training of the linear model?

questions.title: How is feature bagging applied to limit prompt size in FeatLLM?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions using bagging to select a subset of features or instances for each trial, which helps with long prompts when datasets have many columns. I would like to know the exact algorithm: do they randomly sample a fixed number of columns per LLM query, and if so, how is consistency between training and inference maintained when different bags generate different rule sets? Also, how many features are typically sampled for a dataset with >100 attributes?

questions.title: Why does the paper use a linear model without bias after rule generation?
questions.question_body: After converting rules into binary features `z_k^i`, FeatLLM fits a simple linear model (no bias term) to predict class probabilities. Is there an empirical or theoretical reason for omitting the bias? Would adding a bias term improve performance on imbalanced classes, or is it omitted to keep interpretability of rule importance?

questions.title: Clarification on parsing noisy rule text using an LLM (Section 3.2)
questions.question_body: The authors state that instead of writing a complex parser they feed the natural‑language rules back to the LLM to generate Python code that implements them. How is this second‑stage prompting designed to ensure correct translation (e.g., handling variations like "greater than" vs ">")? Are there safeguards against code injection or runtime errors when executing `exec()` on generated code?

questions.title: What does "self‑consistency" refer to in the context of FeatLLM ensembles?
questions.question_body: The ensemble method relies on generating multiple rule sets with high temperature and random demo ordering, and the authors claim this leverages LLM self‑consistency. Could someone explain what self‑consistency means here, and whether any quantitative metric (e.g., overlap of rules across trials) was measured to validate that more consistent rules are indeed more accurate?

questions.title: How is the number of rules per class (R=10) chosen and what happens if R is larger?
questions.question_body: The paper fixes R=10 rules per class after some analysis (Section 4.2). I am curious about the trade‑offs: does increasing R lead to overfitting due to high dimensional binary features in low‑shot regimes, or does it simply increase prompt length without performance gain? Is there any recommendation for adjusting R based on dataset size or feature cardinality?
